content: Each year, approximately one million individuals lose their lives, and around 10 million sustain serious injuries on roads worldwide. Educational interventions aimed at teaching pedestrians how to navigate traffic environments are considered a critical component of injury prevention strategies. Many countries have recommended pedestrian safety education as part of their road safety initiatives. However, given the limited resources available for road safety, it is essential to evaluate the relative effectiveness of various prevention strategies. The primary objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of pedestrian safety education programs in reducing pedestrian-motor vehicle collisions. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Injuries Group's Specialised Register, Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, TRANSPORT, MEDLINE, EMBASE, ERIC, PSYCHLIT, SPECTR, and the WHO database. Reference lists of relevant reviews and studies were also examined, and experts in the field were consulted. The majority of the database searches were performed in 1999, with updates completed in May 2003. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated safety education programs for pedestrians of all age groups. One author screened the records, while two authors independently extracted data and assessed the methodological quality of the trials. Due to significant variability in the types of interventions and outcome measures used across the trials, meta-analyses were not conducted. A total of 15 randomized controlled trials, conducted between 1976 and 1997, were identified. The overall methodological quality of these trials was suboptimal. Adequate allocation concealment was reported in only three trials, and outcome assessment was blinded in eight trials. Additionally, most studies experienced substantial participant attrition during follow-up. Fourteen of the studies focused on children, while one study involved institutionalized adults. Eight studies implemented direct education for participants, while seven relied on parents as educators. Notably, no trials were conducted in developing countries, and none addressed pedestrian safety training for elderly populations. None of the trials evaluated the direct impact of pedestrian safety education on the incidence of pedestrian injuries. However, six trials assessed the effect of these programs on observed pedestrian behavior. Some studies demonstrated evidence of behavioral changes following safety education, but it remains unclear how these changes influence the risk of pedestrian injuries. The authors concluded that pedestrian safety education can enhance children's knowledge and lead to observable changes in road-crossing behavior. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether these changes translate into a reduced risk of pedestrian-motor vehicle collisions or injuries. Furthermore, the observed improvements in safety knowledge and behavior tend to diminish over time, indicating the need for periodic reinforcement of safety education programs.
